## Conclusions

In this research, a novel optimal control strategy of the Hilbert space has been developed to enhance the tracking performance of the non-linear particle swarm optimisation algorithm. The H2PFSAC algorithm is designed to mitigate the curse of dimensionality, which is a limitation of traditional methods. By bridging links between different branches of the search space, it improves particle diversity and, in turn, increases the robustness of the algorithm. The proposed control strategy is evaluated and compared with baseline techniques used in the extant literature using extensive simulations. The proposed implementation of the \(SLS\) technique for vehicle flight control shows promise. However, more extensive research is necessary to ascertain the optimal hardware specifications for the proposed physical realisation of the technique.\textbf{To conclude}\textbf{,}\ \ presents the advantages of this approach. One obvious drawback is that the proposed strategy offers limited scaling.’

- The nominal nonlinear trajectory, the affine error feedback and the dynamic linearization error over-bounds are jointly optimized for robust constraint satisfaction, leading to reduced conservativeness. This formulation leverages and extends SLS to the nonlinear constrained case.
- The reachable set used for robust constraint satisfaction is tight for linear systems with affine feedback.
- The resulting nonlinear optimization problem does not require linear matrix inequalities as in [13], [16], or system-specific offline design as in [4], [5], and allows for an efficient implementation (e.g., using sequential quadratic programming (SQP)), thus ensuring scalability. We demonstrate the conservativeness reduction by comparing with nominal trajectory optimization, open-loop robust trajectory optimization, i.e., without controller optimization, linear techniques [22], [24], i.e., with linear nominal trajectory and offline overbounding, as well as online overbounding of nonlinearity using multiplicative uncertainty (Section IV).

### Over-approximation of nonlinear reachable set

The goal of this section is to decompose the uncertain nonlinear system into a nominal nonlinear system and an LTV error system subject to some disturbance. The linearization of the dynamics (3) around a nominal state and input \((z,v)\) is characterized by the Jacobian matrices:

\[A(z,v) := \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Bigg{|}_{(x,u)=(z,v)},\ B(z,v):=\frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\Bigg{|}_{(x,u)=(z,v)}.\] (6)

Using the Lagrange form of the remainder of the Taylor series expansion, we obtain

\[\begin{xalign*} f(x,u) + w \stackrel{(3)}{\Rightarrow} & f(z,v) + A(z,v)(x-z) + B(z,v)(u-v) \\ &\ \ \ \ \ \ \ +\underbrace{r(x,u,z,v)}_{:=:d}+w, \end{xalign*}\] (7)

with the remainder \(r:\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}}\times\mathbb{R}^{n_{u}}\times\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}}\times\mathbb{R}^{n_{u}}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}}\) where both the disturbance \(w\) and the remainder \(r(x,u,z,v)\) are lumped in the disturbance \(d:=r(x,u,z,v)+w\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}}\). Hence, the overall uncertain prediction is decomposed into a nominal dynamics, LTV error dynamics, and a remainder term, as summarized in Fig. 1.

To bound the remainder, we consider the (symmetric) Hessian \(H_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}+n_{u}}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{(n_{x}+n_{u})\times(n_{x}+n_{u})}\) of the \(i\)th component of \(f\), i.e.,

\[H_{i}(\xi) = \begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial^{2}f_{i}}{\partial x^{2}} & \frac{\partial^{2}f_{i}}{\partial x\partial u}\\ * & \frac{\partial^{2}f_{i}}{\partial u^{2}}\end{bmatrix}\Bigg{|}_{(x,u)=\xi},\] (8)

where \(\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}+n_{u}}\) lies between the linearization point \((z,v)\) and the evaluation point \((x,u)\). We define the constant1\(\mu_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}\times n_{x}}\) as element-wise (worst-case) curvature, i.e., Hessian over-bounded in the constraint set \(\mathbb{P}\):

Footnote 1: Note that \(\max_{\|h\|\infty\leq 1}|h^{\top}Hh|\leq\sum_{i}\sum_{j}|H_{ij}|\), with \(H_{ij}\), the element on the \(i\)th row and \(j\)th column of the matrix \(H\).

\[\mu\eqqcolon\mathrm{diag}(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n_{x}}),\ \mu_{i}\eqqcolon\frac{1} {2}\max_{\xi\in\mathbb{P},\|h\|_{\infty}\leq 1}|h^{\top}H_{i}(\xi)h|,\] (9)

and the error \(e_{k}\eqqcolon(\Delta x_{k},\Delta u_{k})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{x}+n_{u}}\).

**Proposition III.1.** _Given Assumptions II.2 and II.1, the remainder in (7) satisfies_

\[|r_{i}(x,u,z,v)| \xleqq\|e\|_{\infty}^{2}\mu_{i},\] (10)

_for any \((x,u)\in\mathbb{P},(z,v)\in\mathbb{P}\)._

Proof.: Applying the definition of the Lagrange form of the remainder, for all \((x,u,z,v)\) and for all \(i\), there exists a \(\xi\in\mathbb{P}\) (using convexity) such that

\[|r_{i}(x,u,z,v)| =\frac{1}{2}|e^{\top}H_{i}(\xi)e|\]
\[\leq\max_{\xi\in\mathbb{P}}\frac{1}{2}|e^{\top}H_{i}(\xi)e| \stackrel{(9)}{\leq}\|e\|_{\infty}^{2}\mu_{i}.\]

**Remark III.1.** _The evaluation of the constants \(\mu_{i}\) can be achieved using, e.g., sampling, interval arithmetics [32] or tailored nonlinearity bounds as in [10]._

The bound on the Lagrange form of the remainder used in (10) has two factors: the (static) offline-fixed constants \(\mu_{i}\) -the only offline design required for the proposed method- and the (dynamic) jointly-optimized error \(\|e\|_{\infty}\). Crucially, we later co-optimize a dynamic over-bound on the Lagrange remainder (10) with bounds on the error \(e\). Due to Proposition III.1 and Assumption II.3, the combined disturbance \(d\) from (7) satisfies

\[d\eqqcolon w + r(x,u,z,v) \in E\mathbb{B}^{n_{wx}}_{\infty}\oplus\|e\|_{\infty}^{2}\mu\mathbb{B}^{n_{x}}_{\infty}\] (11)
\[= [E,\|e\|_{\infty}^{2}\mu]\mathbb{B}^{n_{wx}+n_{x}}_{\infty}.\]

Using this expression, we can compute an outer approximation of the reachable set of the nonlinear system, using the following LTV error system

\[\Delta x_{k+1} = A_{k}\Delta x_{k}+B_{k}\Delta u_{k}+d_{k}\ \forall k\in\mathbb{N}_{T+1},\ \Delta x_{0}=0_{n_{x}},\] (12)

where \(A_{k}:=A(z_{k},v_{k})\), \(B_{k}:=B(z_{k},v_{k})\) are the Jacobians of the dynamics defined as in (6).

Similar LTV error dynamics are used in [8, 9, 10, 13, 16] to over-approximate the reachable set. To optimize affine error feedback (4) while ensuring robust constraint satisfaction of the nonlinear system based on this LTV error dynamics, we next consider the robust optimal control problem for the special case of LTV error systems as in (12).

\[\Delta x_{k+1} = A_{k}\Delta x_{k}+B_{k}\Delta u_{k}+d_{k}\ \forall k\in\mathbb{N}_{T+1},\ \Delta x_{0}=0_{n_{x}},\] (12)

where \(A_{k}:=A(z_{k},v_{k})\), \(B_{k}:=B(z_{k},v_{k})\) are the Jacobians of the dynamics defined as in (6).

Similar LTV error dynamics are used in [8, 9, 10, 13, 16] to over-approximate the reachable set. ### LTV error dynamics

In this section, we consider the parametrization of linear error feedbacks for LTV systems using established SLS techniques [21], which provides the basis for addressing the nonlinear case via (7). In order to ultimately address the error dynamics (12), we consider a given nominal trajectory \(z_{k},v_{k}\), denote the error \(\tilde{x}=x-z\), \(\tilde{u}=u-v\), and assume the following error dynamics analogous to (12) for ease of exposition:

\[\tilde{x}_{k+1} =\tilde{A}_{k}\tilde{x}_{k}+\tilde{B}_{k}\tilde{u}_{k}+\tilde{u}_ {k}\ \forall k\in\mathbb{N}_{T},\ \tilde{x}_{0}=0_{n_{x}},\] (13)

with \(\tilde{A}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{x}}\times{n_{x}}}\), \(\tilde{B}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{x}}\times{n_{u}}}\), and

\[\tilde{w}_{k}\in\tilde{\mathbb{W}}_{k}:=\tilde{E}_{k}\mathbb{B}^{n_{wx}}_{ \infty},\] (14)

with some \(\tilde{E}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{x}}\times{n_{w}}}\). The notation \(\tilde{\cdot}\) differentiates (13) from the Taylor expansion of the nonlinear system (12). The dynamics (13) are written compactly as

\[\tilde{\mathbf{x}} =\mathcal{Z}\tilde{A}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}+\mathcal{Z}\tilde{B} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}+\tilde{\mathbf{w}},\] (15)

with \(\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\eqqcolon(\tilde{w}_{0},\ldots,\tilde{w}_{T-1})\in\mathbb{R} ^{T{n_{x}}}\), \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\eqqcolon(\tilde{x}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{x}_{T})\in\mathbb{R}^{ T{n_{x}}}\), \(\tilde{\mathbf{u}}\eqqcolon(\tilde{u}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{u}_{T})\in\mathbb{R}^ {T{n_{u}}}\), \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\eqqcolon\mathop{\mathrm{blkdiag}}(\tilde{A}_{1},\ldots, \tilde{A}_{T-1},0_{{{n_{x}}},{{n_{x}}}})\in\mathcal{L}^{{T},{n_{x}}\times{n_{x}}}\), \(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}\eqqcolon\mathop{\mathrm{blkdiag}}(\tilde{B}_{1},\ldots, \tilde{B}_{T-1},0_{{{n_{x}}},{{n_{u}}}})\in\mathcal{L}^{T,{n_{x}}\times{n_{u}}}\) and the block-lower shift matrix \(\mathcal{Z}\in\mathcal{L}^{{T},{n_{x}}\times{n_{x}}}\) is given by

\[\mathcal{Z}\eqqcolon\begin{bmatrix}0_{n_{x},n_{x}}&0_{n_{x},n_{x}}&\cdots&0_{n _{x},n_{x}}\\ \mathcal{I}_{n_{x}}&0_{n_{x},n_{x}}&\cdots&0_{n_{x},n_{x}}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\ 0_{n_{x},n_{x}}&\cdots&\mathcal{I}_{n_{x}}&0_{n_{x},n_{x}}\end{bmatrix}.\] (16)

We introduce the causal linear feedback \(\tilde{\mathbf{u}}=\tilde{\mathcal{K}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\), \(\tilde{\mathcal{K}}\in\mathcal{L}^{T,{n_{u}}\times{n_{x}}}\) i.e., \(\tilde{u}_{k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\tilde{K}^{k-1,j}\tilde{x}_{k-j}\), \(\tilde{K}^{i,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{{n_{u}}\times{n_{x}}}\). Using this feedback, we can write the closed-loop error dynamics as

\[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}=\mathcal{Z}(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}+\tilde{\mathcal{B}}\tilde{ \mathcal{K}})\tilde{\mathbf{x}}+\tilde{\mathbf{w}},\ \tilde{\mathbf{u}}= \tilde{\mathcal{K}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}},\ \tilde{x}_{0}=0_{n_{x}},\] (17)

Abstract In a recent CMS analysis of final states containing events from and , [20] reported limits on cross-quark pair production at the 95% confidence level. Under the assumption that and jets are found only in channels containing a single, hard jet: one quark and quark pair, the measured cross-quark pair invariant mass spectrum will have a strangle-shape at about 150 GeV. The production cross sections of the quark pair and leading (or next-to-leading) jet have a typical deviation from the parton-level cross section that is expected for uncertainties in the factorization and renormalization scales. Several options have recently been suggested for how and jetties can fall into adjacent cells within a QCD femtoscopic box in downstream, jet-selection region. One approach focuses solely on jet energy, while another one combines njet-jet and jet energy with jet-jet . Our calculation applies the former option via its impact on the final state structure: namely, we systematically compute the measured final state cross sections in a control sample with fixed order scale dependence in the NLL accuracy.
